segments.text: When we think about like agent value, so to speak, some people say that the value is actually in the
verification, like whether it did well or not, because that unlocks the next step, which is
automation. If value is derived through verification, who wins? The harness?
If value is derived through verification, I think the people who win are the domain experts,
the people who are able to kind of like quantify what that value means, which is very hard. Like
Building evals is a very hard job.
And so I think a lot of the value will accrue to whoever can kind of like write those verifiers, capture that domain knowledge.
I'm massively bullish on vertical agents for different domains for this reason,
because I think the domain experts who are best suited to write those verifiers or build those evals, as we kind of talk about it,
they will be able to build harnesses and models.
And it won't be just the harness.
It won't be just the model.
It will be some combination of them.
So very practically, if you're getting started building a vertical agent, I would highly suggest you start at the harness layer.
You do context engineering.
You kind of like tweak the harness.
And then when you've got users, then you start tweaking the model in post-training.
I think it's much higher ROI to start at the context or harness layer first.
And so I think we'll have all these different verticals.
They'll be able to quantify what good looks to them in a very domain-specific way.
And that'll let them build not only like vertical agents, but also vertical agent experiences.
Different agents might have different experiences.
